description: We are a team or students that want to explore new things and learn from other people.
summary:
Mars Outpost is a free browser game (no download or account) where kids aged 7-12 run a Mars base. Each day they share limited power between air, food, a storm shield and science. Every choice costs something, and radiation never goes down.

NASA data drives the events. We built a scanner that pulled solar storm records from NASA's DONKI API for 2023-2024. Each mission replays real days, and a storm hits on every day NASA's model predicted a storm cloud reaching Mars; faster clouds hit harder. In emergencies, players can ask Earth for advice, but the reply time is calculated from where Earth and Mars really were on that date, so help sometimes arrives too late.

Space weather is a real hazard for Artemis and future Mars crews, yet it is invisible and hard to explain. The game lets children feel the trade-off between exploring and staying safe. The data is a saved copy, not live, and dust, emergencies and radiation values are game-made and labelled.
details:
What it does and how it works
Mars Outpost is a browser game where kids aged 7-12 run a Mars base. Each day they tap power cells onto four systems: air, food, storm shield and science research. Power is limited, so every cell spent on one system is a cell not spent on another. Once all cells are placed, the day runs and the player sees what happened: air, food, radiation and research change as big icons, with at most three short lines of explanation.

How NASA data is the core of the game
We wrote a browser-based scanner that requests CME (solar storm cloud) and solar particle records from NASA's DONKI API for 2023-2024. It saved a compact copy as a file the game reads. Each mission replays a real run of dates from that copy. On every day when NASA's model predicted a storm cloud reaching Mars, a storm hits the base. Faster clouds hit harder, and the model's arrival-time spread decides how well the player can predict the day. Without the archive, the storms would not exist.

Honest labelling
The data is an archived copy, not live. Dust storms, equipment emergencies, quiet-day surprises and the radiation point values are our own game design. Each is tagged "Game event, not from NASA's log" and drawn differently from real-data cards.

Benefits and intended impact
Space weather is invisible and hard to explain. The game turns it into a visible trade-off between exploring and staying safe, and it shows why Artemis and Mars crews need shielding, forecasts and planning. It is free, needs no account, and is replayable because each mission draws different real dates.

Tools
HTML, CSS and plain JavaScript, with no frameworks and no server. The data comes from NASA's DONKI API via api.nasa.gov, and the signal delay uses JPL's approximate planetary elements (Standish). [AI assistant used for coding help]

What is creative
Real dates replace random numbers as the event generator. Missions grow from 10 to 60 days, and rules unlock gradually (dust and battery, then emergencies, spacewalks) so a 7-year-old can play without reading.

Factors we considered
Plain language, a short play time, no free "safe" choice, and not passing off game-made events as NASA's. A "none logged" day does not mean safe, because the model may simply not have run.
